summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Real estate firms reported 28.0% AI adoption in the latest Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making the sector a measurable but not dominant adopter relative to the broader economy. The growth is incremental rather than dramatic, which tracks with a sector where transaction cycles are long, regulatory exposure is significant, and the consequences of model error can land on household balance sheets.

The oldest and most consequential AI in real estate is the automated valuation model, and it is now federally regulated. FHFA, the CFPB, and the banking regulators finalized binding quality-control standards for AVMs used in mortgage decisions, the first rules of their kind for the sector. Zillow and Redfin publish methodology and error rates for their consumer-facing estimates, which is unusual transparency for production machine learning. Opendoor goes further, running pricing models that carry direct balance-sheet exposure through its iBuying operation, meaning valuation error is not an abstract risk but a capital loss. On the institutional side, HouseCanary and Cherre supply the valuation and data-integration layer that underwrites wholesale transactions. The CFPB's ongoing algorithmic-appraisal work signals that bias and model accountability in valuations will remain under active supervision.

The rest of the documented AI activity concentrates in two places: commercial operations and residential workflow automation. JLL and CBRE deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics at enterprise scale. In commercial buildings, smart-building applications from companies including Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization and predictive maintenance, a pattern the Building Owners and Managers Association tracks across the sector. Matterport's 3D capture creates the spatial data layer that underpins virtual touring and property intelligence. On the residential and multifamily side, EliseAI handles leasing conversations and AppFolio automates property-management operations, while Prophia applies document AI to commercial lease abstraction, extracting rent rolls and obligations automatically. Compass applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and listing recommendations inside the brokerage itself. Proptech capital flows are tracked by the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, CREtech, and MetaProp, and the National Association of Realtors runs its own accelerator vetting which residential tools the profession actually scales.

For anyone deciding whether to deploy, the regulatory picture is the most important variable. AVM use in any mortgage-adjacent context now carries binding federal quality-control obligations, and the CFPB's attention to bias means model documentation and audit trails are not optional. Outside the valuation context, leasing automation and document AI carry lower regulatory complexity and have clearer documented use cases already in production. The sector's moderate and rising adoption rate, the concentration of serious capital consequences in the valuation layer, and the presence of active federal rulemaking together suggest that deployment decisions should start with a clear determination of whether a given application touches federally regulated valuation, and proceed accordingly.
